planting.note: Plant dormant crowns or plug transplants in October in zone 9 for a winter-into-spring crop; Earlibrite is a University of Florida IFAS Gulf Coast Research and Education Center release bred for very early fruit production in the Deep South's fall-planted, short-day plasticulture system, and later served as a parent (crossed with 'Florida Radiance') of the later UF release 'Winterstar'.

directions: Plant dormant crowns or plug transplants with the crown at soil level in raised, plastic-mulched beds in full sun; Earlibrite was released by the UF/IFAS Gulf Coast Research and Education Center in Balm, Florida, bred specifically to ripen its first flush of fruit earlier in the winter production window than the older industry-standard cultivars of its era, giving Gulf Coast growers marketable strawberries before the main season gets underway. As with other short-day cultivars grown in the Deep South annual plasticulture system, set out fresh crowns each fall on raised, drip-irrigated, plastic-mulched beds and treat the planting strictly as a winter annual, since plants decline once summer heat arrives. Earlibrite was later used as a parent (crossed with 'Florida Radiance' in 2005) in the breeding of the UF release 'Winterstar', reflecting its value as an early-fruiting genetic source even after newer cultivars surpassed it commercially.

common_name: Ballerina Indian Hawthorn (Compact Deep-Pink Indian Hawthorn)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring, summer, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade. Ballerina is a compact, dwarf Indian hawthorn cultivar, smaller and denser in habit than older selections like 'Pinkie', bearing deep rose-pink flower clusters in spring above dense, glossy, leathery evergreen foliage, followed by small blue-black berries that attract birds. Its low, tidy, mounding form makes it well suited to foundation plantings, low hedges, and mass plantings where a smaller-scale Indian hawthorn is needed, and it shares the species' reliable tolerance for salt spray, wind, heat, and poor sandy soils. Good air circulation between plants helps minimize the leaf spot disease that can affect Indian hawthorn in humid conditions.

common_name: Halward's Silver Spirea (Compact Silvery-Foliage Nippon Spirea)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Halward's Silver blooms on old wood — prune immediately after flowering (never in fall or late winter) to avoid removing flower buds for the following year.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Halward's Silver is a compact, lower-growing selection of Nippon spirea, noticeably smaller and denser than the species and than 'Snowmound', with fine-textured, blue-gray to silvery-green foliage that gives the shrub a soft, cool color even before bloom. In late spring, flat clusters of small, pure-white, button-like flowers cover the arching branches in the same lace-like display typical of the species, though on a more restrained, rounded mound well suited to smaller borders and foundation plantings where full-size Nippon spirea would be too large. It performs best with consistent moisture and full sun, and light shearing right after flowering keeps the mounded form tidy.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in fall; Duckitt's Yellow is a more restrained, slower-spreading selection than the orange-red species, still forming colonies over time in zones 8b-10 but less aggressively. In zone 8 it may need light mulch protection in cold winters.

directions: Plant corms in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Duckitt's Yellow is a clear-yellow-flowered selection of African cornflag, differing from the typical orange-red species only in flower color and a somewhat more restrained rate of spread. It produces the same upright, sword-like fans of pleated, bright-green leaves and, in late winter and early spring, strongly arching flowering spikes, but the tubular blooms open a clean, bright yellow instead of scarlet-orange, giving a softer, sunnier winter display. The flowers remain attractive to hummingbirds and sunbirds, and established colonies still naturalize over time in zones 8b-10, though less rampantly than the species. Excellent for naturalizing on slopes and banks where a self-sustaining but better-behaved winter color display is desired.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, average to rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Hortensia (commonly sold as 'Golden Glow') is a Victorian-era double-flowered heirloom selection of cutleaf coneflower that has persisted in American gardens, especially old homesteads in the South, since the 1890s.

directions: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, rich to average soil in full sun to partial shade; tolerates more shade and moisture than most Rudbeckia. Hortensia, commonly known as Golden Glow, is a fully double, heirloom cultivar of cutleaf coneflower dating to the 1890s, producing shaggy pompom-like flowers of bright golden yellow on tall, coarse-textured stems from midsummer into fall, without the visible central disc of the wild single-flowered species. It spreads vigorously by rhizomes and can become weedy or invasive in small beds, so it is best sited where it can naturalize freely along fence lines, old homesteads, and the partly shaded edges of rain gardens and stream banks. Division every few years keeps clumps in bounds and reinvigorates flowering; tall stems may benefit from support in windy or rich, over-fertile sites.

common_name: Albiflora Bush Clover (Older White-Flowered Thunberg Lespedeza)

planting.note: Propagate by division or cuttings and plant in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Albiflora is the older of the white-flowered Thunberg lespedeza selections, largely superseded in commerce by the more reliably early- and clear-blooming 'White Fountain' but still grown in older gardens.

directions: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Albiflora is a white-flowered selection of Thunberg's bush clover, the older of the white-flowered forms in cultivation and the standard against which the newer 'White Fountain' selection is measured. Weeping branches clothed in deep green trifoliate leaflets arch outward under the weight of dense racemes of small white pea flowers in late summer into fall, creating the same broad, low fountain of bloom typical of the species, though it can be slower to color up and less consistently bright white than 'White Fountain' as the season progresses. It reaches full size within a couple of growing seasons and, once established, tolerates considerable drought while attracting bees looking for late-season nectar. Because it dies back to the crown in winter in most of its range, treat it as a herbaceous perennial and cut it down before spring growth resumes.
